meta.disclaimer: Research prototype for flight-surgeon support, not diagnosis or approved flight medical guidance. All thresholds, measurement procedures and schedules require mission medical approval. Bands use inclusive min and exclusive max; null is unbounded. Accept whole numbers for heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, SpO2 and mood; allow decimals for temperature and sleep. Reject impossible values, missing values and device errors before classification, including SpO2 outside 0-100, sleep outside 0-24 and mood outside integers 1-5. Glucose bands apply only to fasting readings. Use the worse blood-pressure status. Serious symptoms override every green or amber result. For urgent problems, alert a crewmate and use the onboard emergency protocol while contacting the flight surgeon; do not wait for an Earth reply. These indicators do not measure radiation dose or exclude radiation injury.
meta.unknownStatusAction: No valid reading yet. Log a measurement to see a status.

bodySystems.name: Heart and circulation
bodySystems.spaceflightEffects: PLACEHOLDER: Fluids shift toward the head; the heart can lose mass and blood volume drops.

bodySystems.name: Lungs and breathing
bodySystems.spaceflightEffects: PLACEHOLDER: Cabin oxygen, pressure and air quality affect breathing and blood oxygen.

bodySystems.name: Bones
bodySystems.spaceflightEffects: PLACEHOLDER: Weight-bearing bones can lose roughly 1-1.5% of mass per month without countermeasures.
steps: PLACEHOLDER: Eat your calcium and vitamin D portions.
PLACEHOLDER: Report new back or joint pain.

bodySystems.name: Muscles
bodySystems.spaceflightEffects: PLACEHOLDER: Postural muscles weaken without daily resistance exercise.
steps: PLACEHOLDER: Finish today’s resistance and aerobic sessions.
PLACEHOLDER: Report new weakness, cramps or pain.

bodySystems.name: Immune system
bodySystems.spaceflightEffects: PLACEHOLDER: Immune function can change; latent viruses may reactivate.

bodySystems.name: Eyes and vision
bodySystems.spaceflightEffects: PLACEHOLDER: Spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS) can change vision.
steps: PLACEHOLDER: Run this week’s near-vision card check.
PLACEHOLDER: Note any new blur or headaches.
PLACEHOLDER: Worse than last week? Flag it for your flight surgeon.

bodySystems.name: Mind and behavior
bodySystems.spaceflightEffects: PLACEHOLDER: Isolation, confinement, workload and sleep loss affect mood, cognition and teamwork.

bodySystems.name: Sleep and circadian rhythm
bodySystems.spaceflightEffects: PLACEHOLDER: About 16 sunrises a day in low Earth orbit can disrupt circadian rhythm.

bodySystems.name: Metabolism and nutrition
bodySystems.spaceflightEffects: PLACEHOLDER: Insulin sensitivity and appetite can change in flight.

missionProfiles.name: ISS (low Earth orbit)
missionProfiles.description: PLACEHOLDER: Near-continuous contact with ground and flight surgeons.

missionProfiles.name: Lunar (Artemis)
missionProfiles.description: PLACEHOLDER: About 1.3 s one-way delay; evacuation to Earth takes days.

missionProfiles.name: Mars transit / surface
missionProfiles.description: PLACEHOLDER: 3-22 min one-way delay; crew must act autonomously.

hazards.name: Space radiation
hazards.summary: Radiation can damage cells and raise long-term health risks. Use mission dosimeters; normal vital signs do not prove safe exposure.

hazards.name: Isolation and confinement
hazards.summary: Limited privacy, separation from home and a small crew can strain mood, sleep and teamwork.

hazards.name: Distance from Earth
hazards.summary: Communication delays and limited resupply or evacuation make local assessment and approved onboard care essential.

hazards.name: Altered gravity
hazards.summary: Changing gravity shifts body fluids and changes how the heart, blood vessels, muscles and other systems work.

hazards.name: Hostile and closed environment
hazards.summary: Cabin pressure, air quality, heat, noise, lighting and microbes can affect health. Check environmental systems as well as the person.

indicators.name: Heart rate
indicators.whyItMatters: A changing resting pulse can signal strain, illness, dehydration or an abnormal heart rhythm.
indicators.spaceflightEffect: Fluid shifts and reduced heart conditioning can change pulse. Stress, poor sleep and cabin heat can also affect it.
howToMeasure: Stop exercise and rest quietly before measuring.
Secure yourself in the approved restraint. Keep your arm relaxed and still.
Use the mission-approved monitor. Wait for a stable signal.
If checking manually, feel the wrist pulse with two fingers. Count for 30 seconds and double it.
Record symptoms, recent exercise and whether the pulse feels uneven.

green: Log the reading and compare it with your usual resting pulse.
Report symptoms even if the number is green.
amber: Rest, check the sensor and repeat the reading.
Flag a persistent change or an uneven pulse to the flight surgeon.
red: Stop exertion and alert a crewmate.
Contact the flight surgeon now; use the onboard protocol if unwell.

indicators.escalation: Contact the flight surgeon for a confirmed red result or persistent unexplained amber result. Chest pain, fainting or breathing difficulty needs immediate onboard help at any pulse.
indicators.measureFrequency: Proposed: daily at a consistent resting time, and when symptoms occur.
indicators.reviewNote: AHA supports 60-100 bpm at rest and notes lower athletic baselines. NEWS2 assigns its highest single-parameter score at <=40 or >=131 bpm. Combining these into colors is a proposed rule, not validated astronaut triage. Personalize before use. The restraint step and schedule are proposed microgravity adaptations.

indicators.name: Systolic blood pressure
indicators.whyItMatters: This is the pressure when the heart pumps. Very low or high readings can signal a circulation problem.
indicators.spaceflightEffect: Fluid shifts and heart changes can alter pressure. Returning to gravity can make pressure control harder.
howToMeasure: Use the approved upper-arm monitor with the correct cuff size.
Avoid exercise and caffeine for 30 minutes. Rest quietly for 5 minutes.
Secure your body and support your bare arm in the mission-approved position. Do not talk.
In microgravity, use the same restraint and arm position each time; do not try to plant your feet.
Take two readings one minute apart. Save both systolic and diastolic values from each reading.

green: Log both pressure numbers and compare them with your baseline.
Use the more concerning status from the two numbers.
amber: Check cuff fit and repeat after quiet rest.
Send persistent abnormal readings to the flight surgeon.
red: Alert a crewmate and contact the flight surgeon now.
If stable, recheck promptly. Symptoms need immediate onboard care.

indicators.escalation: A confirmed red result needs immediate flight-surgeon contact. Chest pain, fainting, breathlessness, new weakness, speech trouble or vision change needs emergency care regardless of pressure.
indicators.measureFrequency: Proposed: daily at a consistent resting time; additional checks under the medical plan.
indicators.reviewNote: Low bands use NEWS2 systolic boundaries: <=90 and 91-100. High bands use AHA categories, with >180 marked red. This combined color scheme is not NEWS2 and is not astronaut-validated. AHA normal systolic pressure is <120; the narrower green range reflects the proposed low-pressure alerts. Evaluate paired readings, symptoms and baseline. Microgravity positioning and schedule require approval.

indicators.name: Diastolic blood pressure
indicators.whyItMatters: This is the pressure between heartbeats. Read it with systolic pressure to judge changes in circulation.
indicators.spaceflightEffect: Changes in blood volume and blood-vessel control can change the lower pressure number during and after flight.
howToMeasure: Use the same cuff measurement as systolic pressure; do not measure this separately.
Rest quietly and secure your body and arm in the approved position.
Read the lower number, usually marked DIA.
Save both readings from the paired checks and note any symptoms.

green: Follow the more concerning of the two pressure statuses.
amber: Repeat after rest and check cuff placement.
Report persistent low or high readings, especially with symptoms.
red: Contact the flight surgeon now and alert a crewmate.
Use the onboard emergency protocol if symptoms are present.

indicators.escalation: Confirmed diastolic pressure above 120 needs immediate contact. Low pressure with fainting, confusion or chest pain is urgent even though its numeric band is amber.
indicators.measureFrequency: Whenever systolic blood pressure is measured.
indicators.reviewNote: AHA supports <80 as normal and >120 as severely high. Below 60 is a common low-pressure reference, but no universal isolated low-diastolic emergency cutoff was established. No unsupported lower red cutoff is invented; symptoms and systolic status must override amber. Whole-number inputs are required.

indicators.name: Fasting blood glucose
indicators.whyItMatters: Too little blood sugar can quickly impair thinking. Persistently high fasting sugar needs medical assessment.
indicators.spaceflightEffect: Spaceflight can reduce the body's response to insulin. Activity, food, sleep and stress also affect blood sugar.
howToMeasure: Use these bands only for a fasting check after at least 8 hours without calories, if medically approved.
For symptoms, measure immediately without waiting to fast; flag the reading for clinical interpretation.
Secure the meter, strip, wipes and sharps container before opening supplies.
Clean and fully dry your hands. Use the approved single-use lancet and meter procedure.
Keep the blood drop contained at the fingertip. Apply it to the strip and dispose of sharps immediately.
Record the result, fasting status, symptoms and relevant medicines.

green: Log the result with fasting status.
Keep to the approved meal and exercise plan.
amber: Below 70: if awake and able to swallow, follow the approved low-glucose treatment now.
At 100 or above fasting: report the result; at 126 or above, seek prompt medical assessment.
Do not change medicines or take insulin without the approved medical plan.
red: Alert a crewmate and contact the flight surgeon immediately.
Follow the onboard glucose emergency plan. Give nothing by mouth if swallowing is unsafe.

indicators.escalation: Severe low glucose, confusion, seizure or collapse needs immediate onboard care. Confirmed glucose >=300, or high glucose with vomiting, abdominal pain or abnormal breathing, needs urgent assessment.
indicators.measureFrequency: Only on the flight surgeon's screening plan, or promptly when symptoms suggest a glucose problem.
indicators.reviewNote: CDC supports <70 as low, <55 as severely low, and fasting thresholds of 100 and 126. CDC's persistent >=300 emergency advice concerns diabetes; applying it to astronaut screening is provisional. A single finger-stick cannot diagnose diabetes. Fasting high bands must not classify post-meal readings. Microgravity handling requires the approved biohazard procedure.

indicators.name: Body temperature
indicators.whyItMatters: Temperature changes can signal illness, excessive heat or dangerous cooling. Symptoms and measurement method matter.
indicators.spaceflightEffect: Heat loss changes in microgravity. Core temperature may rise during flight and climb faster during exercise.
howToMeasure: Use the approved thermometer and the same body site each time.
For a routine check, rest after exercise and follow device instructions about recent food or drink.
Secure yourself and the thermometer. Keep the probe steady until the reading completes.
Record the body site, time, symptoms and recent exercise.
Do not treat a skin-temperature sensor as a core-temperature measurement.

green: Log the reading and measurement site.
Report feeling unwell even with a green reading.
amber: Stop exertion, check the measurement and report a persistent change.
Check cabin conditions and follow the medical plan.
red: Alert a crewmate and contact the flight surgeon now.
Use the approved warming or cooling protocol; do not wait for an Earth reply.

indicators.escalation: A red reading, confusion, collapse or suspected heat illness needs immediate care. Report persistent temperature >=38 or a new low reading with illness symptoms.
indicators.measureFrequency: Proposed: daily at the same resting time and whenever fever or heat illness is suspected.
indicators.reviewNote: Below 35 is the NHS hypothermia threshold. Severe heat illness commonly involves core temperature above 40 and neurological symptoms; >=40 is a conservative proposed alert. The 36-38 green window and color mapping require review by measurement site. NASA reports in-flight temperature elevation, so Earth fever references may conflict with personal flight baselines.

indicators.name: Blood oxygen saturation
indicators.whyItMatters: Low blood oxygen can threaten thinking and organ function. A normal reading does not rule out a breathing problem.
indicators.spaceflightEffect: Cabin oxygen and pressure affect oxygen supply. Air contaminants can cause illness that an ordinary oximeter may miss.
howToMeasure: Rest and use the mission-approved pulse oximeter.
Warm a cold hand. Remove nail coverings if the device instructions require it.
Secure yourself, support the hand and keep the sensor still.
Wait for a stable reading and a good signal indicator.
Record symptoms and cabin conditions. If unexpected, recheck another finger without delaying urgent care.

green: Log the reading. Symptoms still need attention.
Do not use SpO2 to judge radiation exposure or carbon dioxide safety.
amber: Check signal quality and repeat while resting.
Report a persistent low reading and check cabin alarms.
red: Alert a crewmate and contact the flight surgeon immediately.
Follow the onboard breathing and cabin emergency protocols.

indicators.escalation: A confirmed red reading or new breathing difficulty, confusion, collapse or blue-grey lips needs immediate assessment. Do not delay care to obtain a better number.
indicators.measureFrequency: Proposed: daily at rest, during relevant symptoms, and as directed after a cabin event.
indicators.reviewNote: Bands use NEWS2 oxygen scale 1 boundaries: <=91 highest score, 92-95 abnormal, >=96 zero score. Colors are a proposed simplification, not NEWS2 scoring or astronaut limits. Other Earth protocols use different thresholds. Cabin pressure, oxygen settings, baseline and device performance require review. Reject values above 100; no high-oxygen toxicity threshold can be inferred from SpO2.

indicators.name: Daily sleep duration
indicators.whyItMatters: Too little sleep weakens attention, judgment and mood. Time in a sleep station is not the same as time asleep.
indicators.spaceflightEffect: Schedules, lighting, noise and stress can disrupt sleep. Astronauts may sleep less than their planned sleep opportunity.
howToMeasure: After waking, estimate total time actually asleep over the last 24 hours.
Include naps and subtract periods spent awake.
Use the approved wearable as a supporting estimate, not a perfect measurement.
Record sleep quality, unusual sleepiness and any sleep medicine.

bands.label: Short sleep; check fitness for duty
Long sleep; check recovery and symptoms

green: Protect the next sleep period and keep a regular schedule.
Report sleepiness even if the total is green.
amber: Check sleep quality, workload, lighting and noise.
Flag repeated changes or daytime sleepiness to the flight surgeon.
red: Tell the crew lead and flight surgeon before safety-critical work.
Use the approved fatigue plan and arrange a protected recovery opportunity.

indicators.escalation: Flag short sleep before safety-critical duties. Uncontrolled dozing, repeated poor sleep or inability to stay alert needs prompt medical and operational review. Red is a fatigue alert, not an emergency diagnosis.
indicators.measureFrequency: Daily after the main sleep period, covering the previous 24 hours.
indicators.reviewNote: Astronaut research links short sleep, including <6 hours, with impaired performance. NASA material supports adequate sleep opportunity and warns about restriction below 7 hours. The 6, 7 and 9-hour color boundaries are proposed operational rules, not validated clinical cutoffs. Long sleep may be normal recovery; no unsupported high-duration red cutoff is assigned.

indicators.name: Mood check-in
indicators.whyItMatters: A private mood check can help identify distress early and support safe teamwork. One score cannot diagnose a mental health condition.
indicators.spaceflightEffect: Isolation, confinement, workload and delayed contact with home can strain mood. Poor sleep can make coping harder.
howToMeasure: Choose a private moment and consider your mood over the last day.
Use the same anchors: 1 very low, 2 low, 3 neutral, 4 good, 5 very good.
Choose one whole number. Do not average away a period of severe distress.
Add a private note about sleep, stress or difficulty doing your usual tasks.
Report feeling unsafe directly; do not rely on this score to communicate it.

green: Keep normal sleep, social contact and private check-ins.
Report distress or unusual behavior even with a high score.
amber: Arrange a private check-in with the flight surgeon or behavioral health support.
Tell a trusted crewmate if stress is affecting your work.
red: Contact the flight surgeon or behavioral health support now.
If you feel unsafe, stay with a trusted crewmate and use the onboard safety protocol.

indicators.escalation: Feeling unsafe, thoughts of self-harm, severe confusion or inability to function needs immediate crew and medical support at any score. Persistent low mood or unusually elevated mood with little sleep also needs review.
indicators.measureFrequency: Proposed: one private daily check-in, with extra support whenever requested.
indicators.reviewNote: The requested 1-5 scale has no established astronaut clinical thresholds in the reviewed sources. Its anchors and 1=red, 2=amber, 3-5=green mapping are explicitly proposed interface rules, not evidence-based diagnostic numbers. Clinical validation, privacy controls and symptom overrides are required before operational use.
